title: Yesterday
job: Past tense — the first big divergence
verifiedBy: Fable (Claude Fable 5) — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: THE divergence of the level, and it is about WHERE the person sits, not about time: the past marks the person with a SUFFIX where M4's non-past marked it with a prefix. dhahabtu (I went) · dhahabta (you went, to a man) · dhahabti (you went, to a woman) · dhahaba (he went) — same stem, opposite end of the word.

Those suffix vowels are written in full because they ARE the person — dhahabtu and dhahabta differ by one vowel and one whole meaning. This never contradicts the no-case-endings rule: what is dropped elsewhere (al-baytu) carries only case; what is written here carries who.

English marks the past on the verb but never the person — "I went", "you went", "he went" are one form. So a learner reaching for anā dhahabtu is translating a pronoun Arabic already put inside the suffix. M1's law, at the other end of the word.

kāna is the verb M1 said was missing, and it was missing only in the present: the past cannot do without it. kuntu fī al-bayt (I was at home) · kuntu taʿbān (I was tired) · kāna al-jaww bārid (the weather was cold). Beside them, the present stays verbless: anā taʿbān.

Full MSA puts kāna's predicate in the accusative — kāna al-jaww bāridan. This course's pause forms hide that ending, deliberately: it carries only case, and the course writes no case endings anywhere. Said aloud so nobody "fixes" it halfway.
ams works like "yesterday": start or end, your choice — ams dhahabtu ilā as-sūq · dhahabtu ilā as-sūq ams. Nothing else moves either way.
hal + the perfect asks "did you…?": hal dhahabta ilā as-sūq ams? English has to bring in "did"; Arabic reuses M2's hal, and the -ta already says you.

Bounded on purpose: no past negation in L1 — MSA needs lam plus a verb shape this level does not teach — so this module stays affirmative, questions aside. (Keeping mā out also keeps it clear of māʾ, one throat-catch away.)

words.note: "Yesterday", standing alone like al-yawm — no preposition. It anchors nearly every sentence in this module, from either end.

M4's adhhab in the past — and the person has moved to the END: dhahab-tu (I), dhahab-ta (you, to a man), dhahab-ti (you, to a woman), dhahaba (he). Same stem as adhhab, opposite end of the word. The final vowel is written because it IS the person.

sentences.trap: The person changed ends of the word: a-dhhab (I go) but dhahab-tu (I went). Prefix in the non-past, suffix in the past.
sentences.sound: AMS dha-HAB-tu i-LAA al-MAD-ra-sa — the -tu is short but never dropped.

variations.cue: I went to school yesterday
variations.changed: ams moves to the end — either seat is fine

variations.cue: Yesterday I went to work
variations.changed: school → work

variations.cue: He went to school yesterday
variations.changed: -tu → -a: he — the shortest suffix in the set, and no pronoun anywhere

mistake.why: English needs its "I", so it sneaks in. The -tu at the end of dhahabtu already says I — anā on top reads as emphasis, not as plain speech.

sentences.usage: The opening line of any account of your day — where you went.
sentences.mnemonic: dhahab-TU: the I went to the tail of the word.

words.note: ashrab's past: sharib-tu (I), sharib-ta (you-m), sharib-ti (you-f), shariba (he). The same -tu/-ta/-ti/-a tails as dhahabtu — one suffix set serves every verb in the language.

sentences.trap: One past event, one cup: bare qahwa. Put al- back on and it becomes that particular coffee — M1's contrast, alive in the past.

variations.cue: I drank the coffee
variations.changed: add al- — that coffee, the one that was there

variations.cue: Yesterday I drank some water
variations.changed: swap the drink, and ams takes the front seat

variations.cue: Did you drink the coffee? (to a man)
variations.changed: hal + -ta: did you — no "did" anywhere, the suffix asks

mistake.why: The English-shaped "yesterday I drink". ams needs the perfect: sharibtu — the person moves to the end of the word, and the prefix form stays in the present.

sentences.usage: What you ate and drank — the small change of any day retold.
sentences.mnemonic: sharibtu rhymes with dhahabtu — every past-I ends in -tu.

words.note: ākul's past: akal-tu, akal-ta, akal-ti, akala. Notice the front of the word relaxed — the long ā of ākul was the I-prefix, and in the past the person left the front for the tail.

sentences.trap: ākul and akaltu are the same verb with the person at opposite ends — front for the non-past, tail for the past.

variations.cue: You ate the fruit (to a woman)
variations.changed: -tu → -ti: you, to a woman — one vowel, new owner

variations.cue: He ate the fruit
variations.changed: -tu → -a: he

variations.cue: Did you eat the fruit yesterday? (to a man)
variations.changed: -tu → -ta with hal in front: the question, to a man

mistake.why: Meant as "I ate", this says "HE ate": akala is the he-form. The I is the -tu: akaltu al-fākiha.

sentences.usage: Retelling meals — with the fruit already on the table, the article points at it.
sentences.mnemonic: akaltu — "I kult(ivated) my appetite": -tu is always I.

sentences.cue: Did you go to the market yesterday? (to a man)

words.note: sūq is the market — the word English borrowed as "souk". s is a sun letter, so the article assimilates: as-sūq, like as-salām. M8 will do its shopping here.

sentences.trap: "Did" has no Arabic counterpart: hal + the perfect does it all, and the -ta of dhahabta is the "you".
sentences.sound: hal dha-HAB-ta i-LAA as-SOOQ AMS — the q of sūq from the very back of the throat.

variations.cue: Did you go to the market yesterday? (to a woman)
variations.changed: -ta → -ti: the question turns to a woman

variations.cue: Yes, I went to the market
variations.changed: the answer: -ta turns back to -tu, I

variations.cue: Did you go with Rohan? (to a man)
variations.changed: the follow-up: maʿa asks about the company, and ams is already understood

mistake.why: Asked of a man, this is wrong: -ti is "you" to a woman. To a man the suffix is -ta: dhahabta. In bare script the two look alike — in this course's spelling, the vowel is the person.

sentences.usage: Catching up on someone's day. The market is where M8's numbers will spend themselves.
sentences.mnemonic: sūq — souk: English already knows this market.

words.note: The verb "to be" exists after all — in the past. kun-tu (I was), kun-ta (you-m), kun-ti (you-f), kāna (he/it was), with the same suffixes as every other perfect. The present never uses it: anā fī al-bayt has no verb, kuntu fī al-bayt must have one.
"At home", learned whole like M4's time phrases: fī ("in") + M3's al-bayt. Written in full — speech says fi l-bayt — and M7 will set fī free as a word of its own, for saying where anything is.

sentences.trap: "Arabic has no verb to be" was only ever true of the present. The past needs kāna, and this is where the slogan dies.
sentences.sound: KUN-tu fi l-BAYT AMS — said, the fī melts into the article.

variations.cue: You were at home (to a man)
variations.changed: -tu → -ta: you

variations.cue: Were you at home yesterday? (to a woman)
variations.changed: hal in front and -ti: the question, to a woman

variations.cue: He was at home yesterday
variations.changed: kuntu → kāna: he — the fourth cell of the row, with nothing else moving

mistake.why: M1's law overextended. The verbless sentence is the PRESENT — "I am at home". Yesterday needs the verb the present does without: kuntu fī al-bayt ams.

sentences.usage: The plainest alibi in the language — where you were.
sentences.mnemonic: kuntu — "I was": the missing verb turns up one tense late.

sentences.cue: I was tired yesterday (said by a man)

words.note: "Tired" — taʿbān of a man, taʿbāna of a woman, the -a following the SUBJECT like every adjective since ṭālib/ṭāliba. The ʿ in its middle is ʿayn. M9 will build feelings on this word in the present, verbless: anā taʿbān.

sentences.trap: Present and past are two different machines: anā taʿbān (no verb) · kuntu taʿbān (verb required). Same adjective, opposite rules.
sentences.sound: KUN-tu taʿ-BAAN — the ʿ squeezes the middle of taʿbān.

variations.cue: I was tired yesterday (said by a woman)
variations.changed: add -a: the adjective follows the speaker being described

variations.cue: I am tired today (said by a man)
variations.changed: back to the present — and the verb vanishes again

variations.cue: Were you tired yesterday? (to a man)
variations.changed: hal + kunta: the question — and the adjective stays bare for a man

mistake.why: Said by a man this is wrong: -a describes a female subject. He says kuntu taʿbān — the agreement law from M1, riding on kāna.

sentences.usage: How yesterday felt. The everyday word — grammars prefer mutʿab, the street says taʿbān.
sentences.mnemonic: taʿbān — tired; taʿab is toil, and taʿbān is what toil leaves you.

words.note: jaww is the weather (and the air); talking about it takes the article, al-jaww, as English does with none. A masculine noun, so its adjectives stay bare: bārid.

"Cold", the winter twin of M3's sākhin, agreeing the same way: bārid with a masculine noun, bārida with a feminine one. Full MSA would write bāridan after kāna — the accusative this course's pause forms deliberately drop.

sentences.trap: kāna in front, and the verbless present sentence (al-jaww bārid) becomes a past one — the verb slots in without reordering anything.
sentences.sound: KAA-na al-JAWW BAA-rid AMS — jaww with a held doubled w.

variations.cue: The weather is cold today
variations.changed: drop kāna and it is the present again — no verb at all

variations.cue: The tea was hot
variations.changed: weather → tea: kāna pushes any verbless sentence into the past

variations.cue: Was the weather cold yesterday?
variations.changed: hal in front of the kāna sentence: was it — nothing behind it moves

mistake.why: al-jaww is masculine, so its adjective stays bare: bārid. The -a belongs to feminine subjects — gender is the noun's own, not the sentence's mood.

sentences.usage: Small talk about yesterday — weather is where kāna earns its keep.

sentences.cue: Yesterday I went to the restaurant

words.note: maṭʿam is a restaurant — the place of ṭaʿām, food, built the way madrasa was built from studying. m is a moon letter, so al- keeps its l.

sentences.trap: kuntu is not an auxiliary: the past lives in dhahabtu alone. There is no Arabic "I did go" or "I was gone" to assemble.
sentences.sound: AMS dha-HAB-tu i-LAA al-MAṬ-ʿam — the ṭ heavy, the ʿ right after it.

variations.cue: Yesterday I went to the market
variations.changed: restaurant → market

variations.cue: Did you go to the restaurant yesterday? (to a man)
variations.changed: hal in front, -tu → -ta: the question

variations.cue: I went to the restaurant and ate
variations.changed: two verbs, two -tu: the outing and the meal in one breath

mistake.why: English "did / was" wants an auxiliary, so kuntu gets drafted. The perfect needs no helper: ams dhahabtu — one verb, person on its tail.

sentences.usage: Recounting an evening out — the sentence every "how was yesterday?" answer starts with.
sentences.mnemonic: maṭʿam — the ṭaʿām (food) place, as madrasa is the studying place.

sentences.display: ams dhahabtu ilā as-sūq maʿa Rohān
sentences.script: أمس ذهبت إلى السوق مع روهان
sentences.cue: Yesterday I went to the market with Rohan
sentences.glossEn: lit. "yesterday I-went to the-market with Rohan"
sentences.literal: yesterday went-I to the-market with Rohan

words.note: "With", for company: maʿa Rohān, maʿa Priyā. A separate word, sitting where English puts it. (The bi- of bi-khayr is the other "with" — the one for tools and manner, glued on; maʿa walks beside people.)

sentences.trap: Company is maʿa, never wa: "Rohan and I went" translates the and, but going along WITH someone needs maʿa.
sentences.sound: ma-ʿa — two light syllables around the throat-squeeze; ma-ʿa ro-HAAN.

variations.cue: I went to the restaurant with Priya
variations.changed: swap place and companion — maʿa holds

variations.cue: I was with Rohan yesterday
variations.changed: kāna + maʿa: where you were becomes who you were with

variations.cue: Were you with Rohan yesterday? (to a man)
variations.changed: hal + kunta + maʿa: where you were becomes who you were with, asked

mistake.display: ams dhahabtu ilā as-sūq wa Rohān
mistake.why: English "me and Rohan went" makes wa ("and") look right. wa joins two sentences or two nouns doing the same job; company takes maʿa: maʿa Rohān.

sentences.usage: Adding people to the story — every outing has a maʿa in it.

sentences.display: ams akaltu al-khubz wa sharibtu al-ḥalīb
sentences.cue: Yesterday I ate the bread and drank the milk
sentences.glossEn: lit. "yesterday I-ate the-bread and I-drank the-milk"
sentences.literal: yesterday ate-I the-bread and drank-I the-milk

words.note: khubz is bread — kh as in Scottish loch, and a moon letter, so al- keeps its l. Here it is the bread of the house, pointed at with its article.

sentences.trap: Each verb carries its own person: akal-tu … sharib-tu. The suffix does not carry over the wa — it is said twice, once per verb.
sentences.sound: AMS a-KAL-tu al-KHUBZ wa sha-RIB-tu al-ḥa-LEEB — one breath, two -tu tails.

variations.display: ams akaltu al-fākiha wa sharibtu al-māʾ
variations.cue: Yesterday I ate the fruit and drank the water
variations.changed: swap both halves — the frame is the story-telling frame

variations.cue: I ate the bread in the morning
variations.changed: ams → fī aṣ-ṣabāḥ: M4's time phrases work in the past too

variations.cue: He ate the bread and drank the milk
variations.changed: both tails turn to -a: he — each verb still owns its person

mistake.display: ams akaltu al-khubz wa sharibta al-ḥalīb
mistake.why: Meant all as "I", but the second suffix slipped to -ta, "you". Each verb owns its person, and both here are I: akaltu … sharibtu — M3's agreement lesson, moved to the tail of the word.

sentences.usage: Two-verb accounts — the shape every "what did you do?" answer grows into (M10 makes turns of it).
sentences.mnemonic: khubz — bread; the kh is the crust.

comprehensionPool.cue: Did you go to school yesterday? (to a man)
I drank the milk in the morning
He went to the market with Rohan
Were you tired yesterday? (to a woman)
I drank a coffee and ate the bread
He went to the restaurant yesterday
Did you drink the coffee in the morning? (to a man)
I was at home with Rohan
Did you eat the fruit? (to a woman)
